conversation: Glad we could all meet before heading out. My family taught me to leave enough fish for next season, and our village depends on this lake. With 100 tons now, we can catch 50 tons between us and leave 50 to double back to 100. How about 10 tons each this month? That’s $10,000 apiece, and we can keep earning that monthly if we stick to the limit. Let’s review our catches together each month and adjust if the stock drops. John, what do you think?

I’m with Luke on this. I learned to fish here with my family, and I want our village’s children to have the same chance. Let’s treat 10 tons each as a firm cap, not a starting point for taking more. If the lake starts a month below 100 tons, we should agree on lower catches before heading out so at least half the stock stays to reproduce. John, would you support that?

Count me in for a firm 10-ton cap. My family has fished this lake for years, and steady income matters more to me than one big haul that leaves our village struggling later. Let’s record everyone’s catch at our monthly meeting so we can see whether we’re keeping our promise. John, are you on board? Emma, I’d like to hear your thoughts too.

I’m in for the 10-ton cap. My family taught me that a good catch means little if there’s nothing left for the village tomorrow. Let’s make any unused share stay in the lake unless we all agree otherwise—one person catching less shouldn’t become an excuse for someone else to exceed their cap. John, can you commit to this plan too?

You have my word: I’ll catch no more than 10 tons this month, and any unused share stays in the lake. My family made a living here, and I want the next generation to have that chance too. That gives us agreement from all five of us. Let’s compare our catches at the end of the month and check the stock before setting next month’s limits.
